en: The Lamp Compendium of Practice (Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa):
Homage to Lokeśvara,
by whose rays of speech [the darkness of] all those who are currently deluded is dispelled.
I bow to that Supreme Person, by whom the lotus of the heart comes to full bloom.
Enlightenment is accomplished by relying upon the perfections and the secret mantra;
since this is indeed the word of the Guru and the Buddha, I shall write down its meaning. (CSP 2)
The secret mantra should not be spoken here; rather, I shall write down in brief the conduct of a bodhisattva who practices the way of the perfections.
The wise person should undertake the vow preceded by the thought of awakening;
having examined all the sūtras, they should listen to the entire treatise.
One should guard the threefold restraints as they have been taught through body, mind, and speech; one should keep the precepts unimpaired and pure, and thoroughly purify them.
One should recognize the proper measure of food and close the doors of the senses;
one should not practice yoga after sleeping during either the first or the last part of the night.
Indeed, one should fear excessively even toward faults as small as an atom;
having divided the night into three parts, one should remain awake during the final part.
One should wash the face and other parts, or even a full washing is appropriate;
having taken a comfortable seat, one should reflect upon the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
When it is impossible [to remain undisturbed] due to agitation caused by signs, one should rise up and,
regarding the objects of appearance as being like an illusion, cultivate the application of merit within that interval.
One should also fulfill the seven limbs and practice the vast vow;
one should cultivate the preliminary meditation at the time of eating.
Seeking the supreme essence with this essenceless body,
one should protect the body as if it were a boat, but not for the sake of physical bulk.
One should not eat out of attachment to flavors; rather, having divided the food into four parts, one should first offer it to the gods, and thereafter to the protector of dharma.
One should offer a very extensive bali-oblation from what remains of one's own food and drink;
and in the interval between [the recitation of] the narrative, one should give [offerings] to all beings.
One should engage in wondrous discourse, or having risen slightly, one should walk about;
one may circumambulate the sacred site, perform recitation, or read from a book. (Csp 14)
One should fashion an image of the Sugata until sweat appears;
during that time, one should perform circumambulations without agitation and make many aspirational prayers. Csp_15.
The ten modes of practicing the Dharma have been taught by Maitreya; in brief, one should practice with an undistracted mind, while recollecting that all things are like an illusion.
If one should honor the Saṅgha, or hold a festival for children, or give excellent gifts to the destitute and to the yogin, that is the accumulation of merit. (Csp 17)

When the duties of the day are complete and during the first watch of the night, one should likewise apply the mind to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), which is free from conceptual proliferation (niṣprapañca). Csp_18 //
And when midnight has arrived, with the perception of the appearance of rising,
one should resort to auspicious sleep, just like the lion’s sleep.
Generally, when the mind is firm in meditation, the merit of body and speech is secondary;
or, when one has not yet touched meditative absorption, it serves for the engagement in worldly activities.
Physical merit should be performed according to one's ability;
when the minds of worldly beings are uneven,
one should act with a virtuous intention, thinking, "This Dharma is not mine alone."
And, urged by his own friend, he inquired about worldly matters;
thus he acted within the realm of Nepal.
If it is not so in the system of the Mantra-yāna, then there is no delight.
Thus it should be done, O Elder.
The *Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa*, composed by the great paṇḍita and master Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna, is completed.
